Author: @paltoth4688
Content:
Another Hungatian here, first of all thx for spreading our long loved gulyás.
However there is one fundamental misrake you MUST avoid and some recommendations.

The mistake was Never put the red paprika in a burning frying pan because it will burn and will get very bitter. You will ruin the whole 5 hours of cooking and you will only know it at the end! Instead turn off the heat wait 1 min and then add the red paprika, mix it and top up with water.

Some recommendations 1. Fry the onions as it adds to the flavour, 2. No need to bland anything just chop the fresh tomatoes and the fresh paprika and put it in the water as in 5 hours they will melt anyway, 3. Ground cumin seedsis a must as that gives the unique gulyás flavour 4 add theBay leaves at the beginning 5. potato is a must with the vegetables, 5 csipetke is made differently. 6. No need for fancy stock as the meat will give you the flavour. 
BuT my biggest suggestion for everyone. USE a pressure cooker for 2,5 hours stopping half way and topping up with watter. After 2,5 hours add all the vegetables and the csipetke and cook normally. This way you half the preparation time and free up 80% of your time.

Most of the time it is served with fresh chilli or some kind of chilli paste. Erős Pista 😂😂

Happy cooking all,

Content:
It looks good, though it is very far from the original recipe.

The original one starts with sautéing the onions on some neutral oil or preferably some kind of lard. After they are just starting to brown, you take it off the fire, and put a fair amount of paprika powder on it, which dissolves in the fat. Back on the fire, then garlic, caraway, then comes the beef. Cook it until the beef gets a good color, then put water on it, and cook it until the beef falls apart. After that, put more water on it, and then put your root vegetables (potato, then carrot, parsley root) in it to cook. When the vegetables are done, it is done.

Author: @EvaCteKnizky
Content:
Interesting how many versions of goulash exist! Here in Czechia, goulash is a beloved food, one of the staples of our cuisine - although it's from another country. Our way of goulash: 
You need the same amount of onions as the meat in weight. Chop finely, fry slowly until brown - that's where the roasted flavour comes from. Add the meat, roast for a bit, let the liquid from the meat evaporate. Add quite a lot of crushed garlic, a lot of dried sweet paprika, generous amount of ground pepper, some ground cumin and some marjoram. You can add some tomato paste.  1-2 minutes of frying it all together, then pour water, salt to taste and let it cook. 
That's basically it. Some people like to add some fresh paprika to have bits of fresh vegetables in it, but mostly it is a fairly homogenous sauce. We eat it with slices of "bread dumpling" and often put freshly cut onion slices on top. It's not as healthy as Adam's version but sooo delicious.

Author: @kapa7197
Content:
Hi, I'm from Hungary. Congrats on the recipe, explained well and most things are spot on. It is hard to criticize because, just like you said, there are many versions of goulash, especially internationally. But since you mentioned traditional hungarian goulash, there are only a few things I'd point out (aside from the food processor, which is pretty unconventional for goulash in Hungary, but I guess why not):
1) It'd be unusual in Hungary to put the dough in the goulash stew. You can certainly eat goulash with many sides such as cooked potatoes or rice or even just bread, but the most common way is to eat goulash with a dough called "galuska", cooked and served separately (or on the side of the plate).
2) A common  technique usually used with goulash is to not use too much water and instead add tiny amounts of it back periodically as it simmers away. Since beef in goulash is cooked for a long time (3-5 hours not unusual on low heat) this technique ensures that nothing gets burnt while still keeping the stew thick and flavorful. 
3) Info if you ever come to Hungary and want to try the stew, you need to order it as "pörkölt". If you order "goulash", in most cases you will get served the soup because waiters don't catch the difference between the english word "goulash" and the hungarian word "gulyás" (which in Hungary usually refers to the soup "gulyásleves").

Author: @eminturksezer9423
Content:
My Hungarian nanny would cry...  No, she would not. First of all you gave the disclaimer and secondly Hungarians are proud that this dish has made into international cuisine and have themselves 50 variations of that dish. In Hungary gulyás is a soup and has a few variations - actually for some people this soup is so thick and savory that they eat as a main dish.

Adam presents a dish that would be called paprikás - one of my favourite base recipes. Again there are lots of variants - famous is carp paprikás. It is one of those dishes that never get's boring.

Tokány is the third jewel in the Hungarian stew crown. The main difference is that the meats are cut into stripes rather than dice. There many, many variations including Transylvanian and Romanian ones.

The "real" goulash is called Pörkölt and is actually probably the easiest recipe. In nutshell you dice 1kg onions which sauté and then pepper with a mix of paprika, caraway powder and majoram. Then you add at least 1/2 l water, wine or like I do dark beer and add 1 kg roughly dice beef calves. Let time do it's magic - dissolve the onions and render out the fat and the gelatin from the meat, add a few gloves of garlic to give a kick and some acid to freshen it up - Adam knows what he does, when he reminds us to do this in other dishes. The result should be fork tendered pieces of meat in a thick dark sauce. I serve the first portion alway with Kaisersemmeln but most white breads with a crunch would work. The great thing is, if you need more just add more onions and meat, just keep the ratio. Boiled or mashed potatoes, Bohemian, Bavarian or Tyrolian dumplings work well with,

If you add cream you get a basic beef paprikás that also works well with egg noodle variant.

Pörkölt has itself variants depending on the meat used. You can leave out the meat and make Paprikás Burgonya just with potatoes.

I do not know how the translation works from Austrian dialect to English, but this video is showing a great base version and gives a few "illegal" variations: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OkG4dAgCg94

Because when it comes to Gulasch, Austrians, Czechs, Hungarians are as strict as Italians can be.

Author: @manfredgrabherr8103
Content:
Hey Adam, as a central/eastern European, I have to say that you got a whole bunch of things wrong. I don't doubt that the food was delicious - just don't call it a Goulash! First, a Goulash in Hungary is a spicy soup, not a stew. What you were aiming for, apparently, is the Viennese Goulash, which is in fact a kind of stew. All it needs is is vegetable oil (not olive), a bunch of onions (not just one), caraway seeds (this is a must), a ton of spicy paprika, garlic if you have it, a really spicy pepper chopped up, and the toughest beef you can find. Add salt and black pepper. After you melt the spices, let cook for 6 hours, stir and refill with water if necessary. Add chopped potatoes if you feel adventurous. 

You best serve this with Knödel, otherwise Nockerln (aka Spätzle). Knödel are super easy to make. Cut up some old stale bread, like baguette, into small cubes, mix a dough of flour and water and two eggs into the dough, add the bread, mix it through until you have a nice consistence. Make dumplings, boil in heavily salted water for 3 to 5 minutes, and there you go.

Now *that* is much closer to the original. Viennese Goulash was a poor people's food. Yet the poor people made something delicious out of it. Wanna try? :)

Author: @david.arpad9
Content:
A couple of things.  Well, several things. Allow me to introduce a Hungarian word: pörkölt. This is the word for the stew that most countries call goulash, and it's also a cooking technique that implies browning. The soup that Hungarians call goulash, or gulyás, starts with a pörkölt. To summarize, both gulyás soup and pörkölt are the same, except with gulyás soup, you add a bunch of water at the end and potatoes, carrots, maybe some celeriac, parsnips or celery root to make it into a delicious soup with a viscous broth.

Pörkölés (the action form of pörkölt) means to cook in sparse liquid until the liquid has cooked away, then to brown a bit before adding more sparse liquid and repeating the process, over and over. That is that canonic way to make goulash as a stew or gulyás as a soup. That doesn't mean that every Hungarian does it that way, but I can pull up a dozen historical and current seminal recipes that do.  There is no need to sear your meat, browning happens during the course of this process, though it obviously can't hurt. This isn't braising, though. Also, pork fat would be preferable to olive oil.

You put all of that delicate paprika into a scorching pan and let it ostensibly burn, which reportedly produces a bitter note. I plan to do A/B testing on this but it is conventional wisdom to remove your pan from the heat until you add liquid. Paprika dissolves in fat and should be added to fat.  That can be to the top of a simmering pan into the fat that has risen to the top or into the fat that the onions have been sauteing in (and then immediately removed from the heat before adding the meat), assuming you would have sauteed your onions. Some chefs do it this way. A smaller contigent swears by blooming the paprika in fat first, before adding it. It only takes 20 minutes for paprika to develop its flavor. It can be added at the end. Many add at the beginning and the end. Also, goulash can often have a little, or a lot, of kick to it. Hot paprika is a thing that many people add, to taste (or hot peppers). I always use hot paprika and sweet paprika and sometimes also, smoked paprika if I'm feeling frisky.

In my opinion, red bell pepper would make it too sweet. Ideally you'd find Hungarian wax or hot peppers, possibly cubanelles as a substitute. The fish sauce was weird but maybe a good idea. I'm always looking for more umami.

Of course your food processor technique is very weird. I don't know what difference that makes at the end. If you pörköl tomatoes, onions and peppers with the meat for 5 hours, they will integrate into the broth, especially if you saute the onions for long enough and peel your tomatoes. Perhaps I'll try it to see what effect it has.

I'm not angry, I just thought I'd add some of my knowledge and experience. This is one of my signature dishes, as a Hungarian who is passionate about Hungarian food and its history, though I'm constantly interested in improving  my version of it.

Content:
Hungarian homecook here.

Okay, first of all, I didn't come here to trash on this recipe. There are some things that Adam got right, and many things he got really wrong. Instead of just leaving a hateful comment like "THAT'S NOT GOULASH", I'd like to explain what the mistakes were. 

First of all, to make goulash, you need to make a Pörkölt. For that you start with pork fat instead of oil, and throw in the finely diced onions. Once they are translucent, and just begin to caramelize, you add the finely diced bell pepper. Get that going, and you can add the cubed tomatoes, then the carrots (I like to shred them, so they dissolve into the sauce), and cook them down, until the moisture evaporates, and it starts frying again. Of course you add some salt with every new veggie, to draw out the moisture. Once it's frying, push them to one side, add the meat and brown it. At this point you can add some tomato paste and get that nice and rusty, and when your meat is almost ready, you introduce the garlic, fry that for a minute or so to open up the flavor. Before anything burns, you pour some water on it. Not much, just to cover everything evenly. You let that simmer for a while, and the fat is going to come out of dispersion, and float to the top. This is the right time to add the paprika. Paprika releases it's flavor and color in fats much much better. It also eliminates the risk of burning your paprika and making it really bitter. Adding it at this stage also helps to thicken the sauce. Now this is what you leave to simmer for several hours, occasionally topping of with a bit of water. Not traditional, and many Hungarians hate this idea with a passion, but during the cooking process, you can use some red wine instead of water, which really boosts the flavor. The pörkölt is done, when the vegetables are all dissolved into the sauce, which at this point should be really thick, smooth and glossy AF. This is when you top it up with more water, add carrots, potatoes and csipetke, maybe some canned kidney beans in the last 5 minutes of cooking, if you want to make babgulyás.

I would like to point out, that it's not a problem to add other ingredients, that you like, as you did with the celery, because no two hungarian grandmas make goulash the same, but the base of all this has to be done right.

Author: @palficsabapeter
Content:
Hungarian here, not mad about the ingredients, even if some of them are untraditional.
What I think most people don't get about the gulyás is the technique that goes into it.

This is a recipe that cattle herders used to make while tending to their flock. As a matter of fact, gulyás literally means the person who is herding the sheep/other cattle.
They would use a pot over a fire to make the dish, and as a consequence of the unpredictable nature of fire, sometimes it would get too hot.

There is a cyclical technique to making this dish where you start off by cooking your ingredients in some kind of fat, and just before it starts to burn, you add some water to prevent it. Thus emulating what those sheep herders would do in those circumstances. Then you keep repeating this, boiling away the water until it starts to cook on its own fat, then adding some water to prevent it from burning, then boiling away the water until it starts to cook on its own fat... You get how this goes.

Since the traditionally used cattle meat (usually the calf of the animal) is a tough piece, you basically do this cyclical frying-boiling thing for at least 3-4 hours. During this, you develop a deep flavour unlike anything else. Then season and set the water level you want and there you go. Gulyás.

Author: @erzsebetkovacs2527
Content: Yay! But this is indeed not traditional Hungarian goulash, it's more like any acceptable American goulash. If you want the genuine article, first, it has to be a thin soup with cubed meat and potatoes, perhaps also carrots in it. No need to use peppers and celery stalks aren't even a thing in Hungarian cuisine. Beef is traditional, but pork would be also fine. No chicken or mutton, though. Second, you don't need to brown the cubed meat and definitely not on olive oil, lol. Use pork fat or any neutral vegetable oil. Third, you start by making a Hungarian meat stew ("pörkölt") base, which then you will water down so that it wouldn't become a "pörkölt", chop up a good amount of onions, and let it cook in hot fat until it gets translucent. You don't need to brown them, and garlic is optional. When the onion gets translucent, pull from the fire, add red powdered paprika and mix well. If you leave it on the fire for this step, the paprika powder may get burnt and bitter. Now you can pull it back on to the fire, add the cubed meat, mix and cook just to the point of the surface or sides of the meat getting white-ish. Again, no need to brown. Now, you can add chopped tomatoes, if you wish, but that ingredient is also optional. Add enough water so that it would be a soup, not a stew. No need to use readily available stock or broth or any other cooking liquid, water is fine. Add the rest of your spices: mainly salt and pepper, but also, optionally, caraway seeds. You can also up the heat at this point and add spicy hot paprika. Let it slowly cook so that the meat would turn soft and easy to chew. When the meat has cooked to your liking, add the cubed potatoes and carrots, if using, and cook until all the solids in the soup get cooked and soft. Now check for taste, and add salt and paprika, if necessary. Hungarians like this soup red with paprika and some Hungarians like it hot. You can serve it with chopped up parsley greens on top, but that's optional. Eat it hot with a slice of good sourdough bread. Enjoy! EDIT: oh, adding "csipetke" is also optional, but traditional.

As a Hungarian I want to clarify a few things:
- Do not let other Hungarians here gaslight you into thinking that Gulyás is exclusively a soup. It absolutely changes depending on region, and in my part of Hungary it is absolutely a stew - if we make it a soup, we call it gulyásleves (goulash soup).
- Blending is unnecessary, and honestly doesn't track with your general approach of making it as easy as possible in the kitchen, and heterogeneity. Just rough chop and cook long enough that everything falls apart, some slight chunks are fine.
- Fish sauce is crazy work
- Parsley root and parsnips are basically the same thing, at least close enough, so don't feel bad about substituting.
- Finished product looks great, still more authentic than what they call goulash in Czechia

Author: @PrOmArTiN007
Content:
As a born-and-raised Hungarian, I feel like I should tell you exactly how we make authentic goulash soup, because you overcomplicated it a bit with that blender stuff.
Overall, though, it's closer to the real thing than I expected — so congratulations, Adam!

Ingredients:
150 g pork lard
1 kg beef (we usually use beef shin, but tri-tip looks fine — it should be gelatinous, as you said)
3 large onions, diced (we use a lot of onion)
4–5 cloves garlic, finely chopped or smashed
3 sweet Hungarian yellow peppers, diced (bell peppers have a very different taste, but I get that that’s all you have available, so it’s “fine”)
2 large tomatoes, diced
400 g potatoes, diced
3 large carrots, sliced
1 large parsnip or turnip, sliced
1 medium celeriac, diced (not celery — celeriac, big difference!)
2 tbsp powdered caraway seeds
Hungarian sweet paprika (a lot — but let’s say 40 g for now; the more, the better)
Pepper
Salt
2–3 bay leaves
Fresh parsley

The csipetke is GREAT — didn’t see that coming, Adam, so that’s a big plus!
It’s optional, but if I were you, I’d prepare it in a bowl while the meat is simmering because it can be very time-consuming. You can dust it with a bit of flour so it doesn’t stick together while the soup is simmering.
Also, you should pinch off a little bit of dough and roll it into a small ball — just like when you were a kid picking your nose. The way you did it looks more like dumplings than csipetke, but still, good try!

Instructions:
1. Use 50 g pork lard to brown the meat in a pot with some salt and black pepper.
2. Take out the meat, then add the remaining 100 g lard and slowly sweat the onion with a pinch of salt until translucent.
3. Add the garlic.
4. When you can smell the garlic, turn off the heat and stir in the paprika (if you leave it on the heat, it can easily burn).
5. Add the meat back, along with the 2 tbsp powdered caraway seed, bay leaves, pepper, and tomato, plus a pinch of salt.
6. Stir, cover with a lid, turn on the heat to low.
7. When the pepper and tomato release some water, stir again, and add enough water for it to be a soup, put the lid back and bring it to a boil — taste and adjust seasoning if needed.
8. When it just started to boil, bring the heat to low and let it simmer until the meat is tender, keep on the lid.
9. Before it’s fully done, add the vegetables (carrots, parsnip/turnip, celeriac, potatoes), put on the lid, bring it to a boil.
10. When it just started to boil, bring the heat to low and let it simmer until the vegetables are fork-tender, keep on the lid.
11. When the vegetables are fork-tender, it’s almost ready, you can add the csipetke if you made some, keep the lid on.
12. When the csipetke is ready, adjust the seasoning one last time if needed.
13. Turn off the heat, add the fresh parsley, stir one more time, and serve.

We usually eat it with bread, dunked in the soup, if there’s no csipetke.

Anyway, this is a surprisingly great goulash soup, Adam — good job! :D

Author: @ludwigziffer6895
Content:
My goulash game improved significantly when I started treating it like French onion soup with meat.
Start by searing your goulash meat in the pot but make absolutely sure nothing scorches or the whole dish goes bitter. Take out the meat, then in goes a whole bag of yellow onions (those big white onions you Americans use don't have nearly as much flavor as the small yellow ones and you can *really* taste the difference in this), medium diced. Let those go for like an hour, low heat, you want them to caramelize super slowly, so that they're breaking down into a sludge. A spoonful of flour to thicken the whole thing, then a couple cloves of garlic, whole.
Once the onions have completely broken down, add the meat back in, fill the pot up with a lot of water and let it cook for at least two hours. While it cooks you can add as much paprika, salt and pepper as you so choose, though I'd hold back on all three, lest they overpower the delicate flavor of the onions and the mellow sweetness of the garlic.
